title: Your Laugh Is a 15-Million-Year-Old Echo!
summary: Have you ever laughed so hard your belly hurt? That silly sound might be way older than you think. Scientists just discovered that the rhythm of human laughter has been around for at least 15 million years! They compared laughs from humans, orangutans, gorillas, bonobos, and chimpanzees. All of them laughed with evenly spaced sounds—like a steady drumbeat. This means our last common ancestor, who lived long before any humans walked the Earth, probably laughed the same way. Dr. Chiara De Gregorio from the University of Warwick says, 'We've found a 15-million-year-old clue in an unexpected place: our laughter.' But human laughter is special. We can change it depending on how we feel. A tickle laugh is different from a polite laugh at a joke you don't really get. Other apes can't do that as well. Over millions of years, our ancestors got better at controlling their voices. That skill might have helped us learn to talk! Since speech doesn't leave fossils, laughter is like a window into the past. It shows that the path to talking wasn't a sudden jump—it was a slow, steady climb. So next time you crack up, remember: you're sharing a rhythm that's older than the dinosaurs!
why_it_matters: Your laugh connects you to ancient ancestors and shows how slow changes over time made human speech possible.

background_read: All great apes, including humans, share a common ancestor that lived millions of years ago. Scientists can study how we evolved by comparing behaviors like laughter, which doesn't leave bones but can point to deep family ties.
Dr. Chiara De Gregorio (a researcher at the University of Warwick in England) helped show that the steady beat of laughter is older than we thought.
This kind of work helps us understand how human speech might have developed step by step, even without ancient voice recordings.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists like Dr. Chiara De Gregorio, humans, orangutans, gorillas, bonobos, and chimpanzees.
WHAT: The rhythm of laughter is the same across great apes, meaning it goes back at least 15 million years to a common ancestor, and it may help explain how speech evolved.
WHERE: Across the great apes on Earth, with research at the University of Warwick.
WHY: Because speech doesn't leave fossils, studying laughter shows that the path to talking was a slow, steady climb over millions of years.

perspectives.description: It's amazing to think our silly laughs are part of a 15-million-year-old story, linking us to our ape cousins.
Scientists see laughter as a clue, but not everyone agrees it directly explains how speech evolved—it's just one piece of a big puzzle.
This might lead to more research on how our voices changed, helping us understand what makes humans unique.
